meaning: The Nile flood god Hapi; from ḥꜥpj

phonemes.desc: Voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ] — a strong breath scraped from the throat, unlike English h — plus a long open vowel.
Voiceless bilabial stop plus short close front vowel; the conventional vocalization of the final weak consonants.

pronunciation.approximation: HAH-pee; the ḥ is a strong breath, not a plain h.
pronunciation.note: ḥp is conventionally vocalized "Hapi"; the ḥ (Gardiner Aa1) is the pharyngeal fricative heard at the start of the name. He must not be confused with Ḥpy the baboon-headed son of Horus — same sound, different god: the restoration keeps the underdot that marks the river-lord's true name.

domains.title: The Flood that Feeds
domains.subtitle: The Inundation, Abundance, and the Fat of the Land
domains.lead: ḥp is the Nile flood personified: the annual miracle on which all of Egypt hung, arriving as a blue-green, androgynous, heavy-bellied bringer of plenty. No temple was built to him — he needed none; the river was his temple, and its rising his epiphany.

cards.name: The Inundation
cards.desc: The akhet season: the river rising to feed the black land — Egypt's single most sacred event.

cards.name: The Offerings
cards.desc: He bears trays of fish, fowl, and produce — the land's abundance carried in his own arms.

cards.name: The Sema-Tawy
cards.desc: The double Hapi tying papyrus and lotus around the windpipe-sign: the Two Lands knotted into one.

cards.name: The Nilometer
cards.desc: His measure at Elephantine: cubits of rise that set the year's tax and the year's hope.

mythology.lead: ḥp has no adventures because he is not a character but an event: the flood. His mythology is hydrology made sacred — the river's rhythm given a face, a hymn, a nilometer, and a table of offerings. What the Greeks would later read as myth, Egypt experienced as the annual audit of its own survival.

myths.title: The Hymn to Hapi
myths.text: The great Hymn to Hapi — copied by schoolboys for a thousand years, its finest witnesses New Kingdom papyri (Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature, vol. 1) — is the flood's own voice. It calls him 'lord of fish and fowl, maker of barley, creator of wheat,' and praises the land's dependence in the plainest economics ever put into verse: when he rises, 'the whole land rejoices'; when he fails or arrives thin, 'the whole land is in panic' and the granaries stand empty. The hymn lists what every Egyptian saw with his own eyes: the water turning black with silt, the fields greening in days, the tax assessors waiting on the bank. No temple was ever his — the river was the temple — and no statue could be more present than the water itself. The hymn means that ḥp was worshipped the way weather is feared: not in a shrine but at the water's edge, where plenty and famine were decided on the same bank.

myths.title: The Tying of the Two Lands
myths.text: On temple walls from Karnak to Dendera, ḥp appears doubled: one figure crowned with the papyrus of the Delta, one with the lotus of the south, the two of them knotting the plants around the hieroglyph of the windpipe — sema-tawy, 'the uniting of the Two Lands.' The image is everywhere because it says everything: Egypt is not two countries with a god each but one body with one flood. The device is already Old Kingdom; it climbs onto royal thrones, onto the sides of ceremonial footstools, into the ground-plans of temples, until the nation's founding act — the union of Upper and Lower Egypt — is performed annually by the rising water. The two ḥp-figures do not fight, as the Two Lands' emblematic plants sometimes do elsewhere in Egyptian art; they tie the knot together. The myth means that the flood was Egypt's constitution written in vegetation: sovereignty, like the river, flowed from south to north and had to be re-knotted every year.

myths.title: The Caverns of the Nile
myths.text: Where did the flood come from? Egyptian geography said the First Cataract at Elephantine, and Egyptian imagination supplied the rest: subterranean caverns beneath the island where the ram-headed potter Khnum sat at his wheel, shaping the flood and with it the bodies of kings — the tale of Khnum's claim is enshrined on the Ptolemaic Famine Stela at Sehel Island. ḥp dwelt in those cavern-waters with the earth-god and the abyss; the cataract's granite roar was the sound of the flood's door opening. Later geographers pushed the source farther south, to fabulous 'Mountains of the Moon,' but the theology mattered less than the observation it framed: the river rose at the solstice as Sirius returned, and every calendar, tax roll, and liturgy bent to its timing. The myth means that the Egyptians did not need to see the source to know it was sacred: the regularity itself was the miracle, and regularity is the oldest form of theology.

myths.title: The Blood of Osiris
myths.text: Greek witnesses saw deeper into the flood than measurement. Plutarch, in On Isis and Osiris (32–36), reports the Egyptian doctrine that the Nile itself was the god: its waters called the 'efflux of Osiris,' its life-giving rise the murdered god's generative return, its failure and muddy retreat the work of Typhon. The flood that made the fields fertile was thus, in the late theology, the same event as the god's resurrection — Osiris's body dispersed and recomposed as water. This is why the mourning of Isis and the rising of ḥp could be read as one story told in two registers, and why tomb walls pair the two so comfortably. Plutarch wrote five centuries after the last native pharaoh, and scholars rightly caution that his account blends philosophy with reportage; but the identification had Egyptian roots, not merely Greek ones. The myth means that the Egyptians did not separate agriculture from resurrection: the black silt of June was a god coming back to life on schedule.

lore.syncretism: The Greeks called him Neilos and gave the river-god a Greek biography — making him, in some accounts, father of Memphis and ancestor of the Danaid line that returned to Argos. The word "Nile" itself descends through this identification. In Nubia he merged with local flood-lords; in the Fayum, his abundance fed the crocodile cult of Sobek, whose lake was the flood's great reservoir. Every downstream culture read the same rising water and named its own god.
lore.culturalLegacy: He is the reason Egyptology has a tax-system to study: nilometer readings governed assessments, and the "perfect flood" — about 16 cubits at Memphis — was the single most important number in the ancient economy. The Aswan High Dam ended his annual epiphany in 1970: the fields no longer drown, and Egypt marks the loss in every history of the river. "Hapi" survives in countless modern Egyptian names and in the eco-memory of a regulated Nile.
lore.extendedMeditation:
ḥp is the god of the right amount. Too little and Egypt starved; too much and it drowned: his theology is the arithmetic of enough. Every flood-forecast, every reservoir, every rationing scheme since is his liturgy translated — the oldest question of abundance is not how to get more, but how to receive what comes.

The dam ended his flood in a single generation, and Egypt's ambivalence about the Aswan High Dam is his modern myth: the silt no longer comes, the fields are fed by chemistry, the delta retreats — and no one would vote to bring the drowning back. ḥp's question outlives his river: abundance engineered is abundance owed to what? The flood that fed for five thousand years was never free; it was merely invoiced in a currency — rhythm, silt, patience — that modernity is only now learning to price again.

The hymn says it plainly: when he rises, the land rejoices; when he fails, the temples themselves seem to close. Egypt knew what every river civilization relearns — the water is not a resource but a relationship, renewed annually or not at all. The nilometer's cubits were the oldest economic forecast in the world, and the tax register waited on the river like a priest on an oracle.

lore.archaeology: Nilometers survive at Elephantine (a stairwell of cubit scales rebuilt under the Romans), at Roda island in Cairo (the famous octagonal shaft, Abbasid-era over Fatimid work), and at Philae. His iconography is among the most common in Egyptian art: the procession of fat-bellied offering-bringers lines the base of temple walls from Karnak to Dendera, and the double-ḥp sema-tawy decorates royal thrones from the Old Kingdom onward. The Hymn to Hapi's best copies come from school texts — pupils learned the river's praise by heart.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written ḥ-p with the water sign and the determinative of the fat-bellied offering-bringer; in the fullest orthographies the name rides in the Hymn to Hapi's papyrus copies. The god himself — blue-skinned, heavy-breasted, crowned with papyrus or lotus — is his own determinative: abundance in human form.
